lessons.title: Particle Model, Density and Pressure
lessons.description: Density of solids, liquids and gases, changes of state, and pressure in fluids and gases.
lessons.content_html:
The Particle Model of Matter

The particle model explains the properties of solids, liquids and gases in terms of how their particles are arranged and how they move. In a solid, particles are held in fixed positions in a regular arrangement by strong forces between them. They vibrate about fixed points but cannot move from place to place — this explains why solids have a fixed shape and a fixed volume.

In a liquid, particles are close together but can slide past each other because the forces between them are weaker than in a solid. Liquids have a fixed volume but take the shape of their container. In a gas, particles are far apart with negligible forces between them. They move rapidly in random directions, colliding with each other and the walls of their container. Gases fill any container and can be compressed because of the large spaces between particles.

Key Fact

In a solid, particles are in fixed positions (vibrating only). In a liquid, particles are close but can flow past each other. In a gas, particles are far apart and move randomly. Gases can be compressed because of the large spaces between particles; solids and liquids cannot.

What Is Density?

Density tells you how much mass is packed into a given volume. A dense material has a large amount of mass in a small volume. The equation is:

$$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$$

Where \(\rho\) is density (\(\text{kg/m}^3\) or \(\text{g/cm}^3\)), \(m\) is mass (kg or g), and \(V\) is volume (\(\text{m}^3\) or \(\text{cm}^3\)). You must be able to rearrange the equation to find mass (\(m = \rho \times V\)) or volume (\(V = \frac{m}{\rho}\)). To convert between units: \(1 \text{ g/cm}^3 = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3\). A common exam error is failing to convert grams to kilograms before calculating in SI units.

Question: A metal cube has a mass of 216 g and a volume of \(80 \text{ cm}^3\). Calculate its density in \(\text{g/cm}^3\).

Answer: Write the equation: \(\rho = \frac{m}{V}\). Substitute: \(\rho = \frac{216}{80} = 2.7 \text{ g/cm}^3\). This is the density of aluminium. To express in SI units: \(2.7 \text{ g/cm}^3 = 2700 \text{ kg/m}^3\).

Measuring Density (PAG P1)

To measure the density of a regular solid (such as a cuboid), measure its mass on a balance and calculate its volume using a ruler: \(V = l \times w \times h\). For a cylinder, use \(V = \pi r^2 h\). Then apply \(\rho = m/V\).

For an irregular solid (such as a pebble), use a displacement method. Fill a eureka can until water overflows at the spout. Gently lower the object into the water and collect the displaced water in a measuring cylinder — its volume equals the volume of the object. Alternatively, use a measuring cylinder directly: record the initial water level, submerge the object, and measure the new level. The volume of the object equals the rise in water level.

For a liquid, measure the mass of an empty measuring cylinder, pour in the liquid, and measure the total mass. The liquid’s mass is the difference. Read the volume from the graduated scale at the bottom of the meniscus. Apply \(\rho = m/V\).

Key Fact

Density of a regular solid: measure mass and calculate volume using a ruler, then \(\rho = m/V\). Density of an irregular solid: measure mass on a balance, find volume by water displacement (eureka can or measuring cylinder), then apply \(\rho = m/V\). Read the measuring cylinder at the bottom of the meniscus.

Why Densities Differ

The particle model explains why densities differ between states of matter. In solids, particles are closely and regularly packed, giving high density. In liquids, particles are slightly further apart and less ordered, so density is a little lower. In gases, particles are very widely spaced, so density is dramatically lower — typically about a thousand times less than the same substance in liquid form. Crucially, mass is conserved during any change of state: the number of particles does not change, only their arrangement and spacing. When ice melts to water, the same particles are present but occupy a slightly different volume. When water boils to steam, the vast increase in volume means density falls dramatically.

An important exception is water: ice is slightly less dense than liquid water, which is why ice floats. This unusual behaviour occurs because water molecules form an open lattice structure in the solid state, taking up more volume per molecule than in the liquid state.

Pressure in Fluids

Pressure in a gas arises because gas particles constantly collide with the walls of their container, exerting a force on each unit of area. In a liquid or gas (both are fluids), pressure acts in all directions and increases with depth below the surface. The qualitative reason is that a deeper column of fluid has more weight of fluid above it pressing down, increasing the force on any surface at that depth.

For Higher tier, the pressure at a depth in a fluid can be calculated using:

$$p = h \times \rho \times g$$

Where \(p\) is pressure (Pa), \(h\) is the depth of the fluid (m), \(\rho\) is the density of the fluid (\(\text{kg/m}^3\)), and \(g\) is the gravitational field strength (10 N/kg on Earth). This equation shows that pressure increases with depth (greater \(h\)), with denser fluids (greater \(\rho\)), and in stronger gravitational fields. For example, a diver at 10 m depth in sea water (density approximately \(1025 \text{ kg/m}^3\)) experiences a pressure of \(p = 10 \times 1025 \times 10 = 102{,}500 \text{ Pa}\) from the water alone, in addition to atmospheric pressure above.

Worked example: A submarine is at a depth of 200 m in sea water (\(\rho = 1025 \text{ kg/m}^3\)). Calculate the pressure due to the water at this depth. \(p = h\rho g = 200 \times 1025 \times 10 = 2{,}050{,}000 \text{ Pa}\) (or 2.05 MPa). Always state the unit — pascals (Pa) — in the final answer.

Key Fact

Pressure in a gas is caused by particles colliding with the container walls. Heating a gas at constant volume increases particle speed, so collisions become more frequent and more forceful — pressure rises. In a fluid column, pressure increases with depth.

Heating a gas at constant volume increases the kinetic energy of the particles. They move faster, collide with the container walls more frequently, and each collision exerts a greater force. Both effects increase the pressure. This is why sealed containers such as aerosol cans carry warnings about exposure to heat — the rising pressure could exceed the container’s strength and cause it to burst.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For density calculations, always show the equation, substitution and units. A very common error is failing to convert grams to kilograms (or g/cm³ to kg/m³) when working in SI units — always check before calculating. For the displacement experiment with an irregular solid, describe the procedure step-by-step: place water in cylinder, record initial level, submerge object fully, record new level, subtract to find volume. For pressure in fluids at Higher tier, make sure you include the unit — Pa (pascals) — in your final answer.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The particle model explains the properties of solids (fixed arrangement, vibrate only), liquids (close but can flow) and gases (widely spaced, rapid random movement). Gases have the lowest density; solids the highest.
  • Density = mass ÷ volume. For regular solids, measure dimensions with a ruler; for irregular solids, use water displacement. Mass is always conserved during changes of state.
  • Pressure in a gas arises from particle collisions with container walls. In a fluid column, pressure increases with depth. At Higher tier, fluid pressure is calculated using p = hρg.

lessons.title: Internal Energy, SHC and Latent Heat
lessons.description: Specific heat capacity, specific latent heat of fusion and vaporisation, and heating curves.
lessons.content_html:
Changes of State

Matter can change between three states — solid, liquid and gas. These are physical changes: they are reversible and no new substance is formed. Crucially, mass is conserved during any change of state — the same particles are present before and after; only their arrangement and spacing change.

The key changes of state are: melting (solid to liquid), freezing (liquid to solid), evaporation/boiling (liquid to gas), condensation (gas to liquid), and sublimation (solid directly to gas). Evaporation occurs at the surface of a liquid at any temperature — the fastest-moving particles at the surface escape as gas. Boiling occurs throughout the entire liquid at a specific temperature when enough energy is supplied. Evaporation causes cooling because the most energetic particles leave, reducing the average kinetic energy of those remaining.

Key Fact

Changes of state are physical, reversible changes that conserve mass. Evaporation occurs at the surface at any temperature; boiling occurs throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature. Both transfer particles from liquid to gas state.

Internal Energy

When you heat a substance, you increase its internal energy. Internal energy is the sum of the kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles in the substance. It is important to distinguish between temperature and internal energy: temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles, while internal energy includes both kinetic and potential contributions from every particle.

Heating a substance can do one of two things. If the substance remains in the same state, the energy increases the kinetic energy of the particles — they move faster and the temperature rises. If a change of state is occurring, the energy instead increases the potential energy of the particles by breaking the forces between them (or forming them during cooling), and the temperature stays constant during this process.

A heating curve shows temperature on the y-axis against time (or energy supplied) on the x-axis. The graph has sloping sections, where temperature rises (kinetic energy of particles increases), and flat sections (plateaus), where the temperature stays constant while a change of state occurs (potential energy changes as bonds between particles are broken or formed).

The first plateau is at the melting point (solid changing to liquid). The second plateau is at the boiling point (liquid changing to gas). During each plateau, the substance exists as a mixture of two states. The length of each plateau depends on the specific latent heat of the substance for that change of state — a longer plateau means more energy is needed to complete the transition. The gradient of the sloping sections depends on the specific heat capacity — a shallower slope indicates a higher specific heat capacity (more energy per degree).

Specific Heat Capacity

Specific heat capacity (SHC) quantifies how much energy is needed to heat a given mass of material. Different materials require different amounts of energy for the same temperature rise. Water has a high SHC of 4200 J/(kg °C), meaning it takes a large amount of energy to heat it — which is why it is used in central heating systems and why coastal regions have more moderate climates than inland areas.

The equation linking energy change to temperature change is:

$$\Delta E = m \times c \times \Delta \theta$$

Where \(\Delta E\) is the change in thermal energy (J), \(m\) is mass (kg), \(c\) is the specific heat capacity (J/(kg °C)), and \(\Delta \theta\) is the temperature change (°C). You must be able to rearrange this equation — for example, \(c = \frac{\Delta E}{m \times \Delta \theta}\) or \(\Delta \theta = \frac{\Delta E}{m \times c}\). Always check units before substituting.

Question: How much energy is needed to heat 2.0 kg of water from 20 °C to 80 °C? (SHC of water = 4200 J/(kg °C))

Answer: \(\Delta \theta = 80 - 20 = 60\) °C. \(\Delta E = m \times c \times \Delta \theta = 2.0 \times 4200 \times 60 = 504{,}000\) J = 504 kJ.

To investigate the SHC of a metal block: drill two holes in the block — one for a thermometer and one for an electrical immersion heater. Measure the block’s mass using a balance. Record the starting temperature, switch on the heater, and record the energy supplied using a joulemeter and the final temperature when heating is stopped. Rearrange to find \(c = \frac{\Delta E}{m \times \Delta \theta}\). The main source of error is heat lost to the surroundings; wrapping the block in insulating material (lagging) reduces this. This PAG also involves comparing the SHC of water and aluminium.

Key Fact

Specific heat capacity equation: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\). SHC is measured in J/(kg °C). Water has a high SHC (4200 J/(kg °C)), requiring a large energy input for a small temperature rise — making it ideal for central heating and thermal energy storage.

Specific Latent Heat

Specific latent heat (SLH) is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance at constant temperature. There is no temperature change during the process — all the energy goes into breaking or forming the intermolecular forces between particles. There are two types:

• Specific latent heat of fusion (\(L_f\)) — the energy needed to change 1 kg of a substance from solid to liquid at its melting point (or released when it freezes). For water, \(L_f = 334{,}000 \text{ J/kg}\).
• Specific latent heat of vaporisation (\(L_v\)) — the energy needed to change 1 kg from liquid to gas at its boiling point. For water, \(L_v = 2{,}260{,}000 \text{ J/kg}\).

The latent heat of vaporisation is always much greater than the latent heat of fusion for the same substance, because particles must fully overcome the intermolecular forces to become a gas (much more energy is needed than just separating them partially as in melting). The equation relating thermal energy to a change of state is:

$$E = m \times L$$

Where \(E\) is the thermal energy for the change of state (J), \(m\) is mass (kg), and \(L\) is the specific latent heat (J/kg).

Question: How much energy is needed to completely melt 0.5 kg of ice at 0 °C? (\(L_f\) for water = 334 000 J/kg)

Answer: \(E = m \times L_f = 0.5 \times 334{,}000 = 167{,}000 \text{ J}\) (or 167 kJ). Note: the temperature stays at 0 °C throughout the melting process.

Key Fact

Specific heat capacity (SHC) — involves a temperature change, no state change: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\). Specific latent heat (SLH) — involves a change of state at constant temperature: \(E = mL\). The latent heat of vaporisation is always much larger than the latent heat of fusion.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The most common error in SHC calculations is using the total temperature rather than the change in temperature (\(\Delta\theta\)). Always subtract the initial temperature from the final temperature first. For latent heat questions, remember that temperature stays constant during a change of state — if a question asks you to calculate energy for melting or boiling, use \(E = mL\), not \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\) (there is no \(\Delta\theta\) term because temperature does not change). Make sure you state units in all final answers — J or kJ for energy.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Internal energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energy of all particles. Heating raises temperature (more kinetic energy) or causes a change of state (more potential energy at constant temperature). Heating curves show these as sloping sections and flat plateaus respectively.
  • Specific heat capacity (\(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\)) is the energy needed to raise 1 kg by 1 °C without changing state. Water’s high SHC (4200 J/(kg °C)) makes it useful for heating systems.
  • Specific latent heat (\(E = mL\)) is the energy for a change of state at constant temperature. Latent heat of vaporisation is always much greater than latent heat of fusion because more energy is needed to fully separate particles into a gas.

lessons.title: Motion: Speed, Velocity and Acceleration
lessons.description: Distance-time and velocity-time graphs, speed, velocity, acceleration, and terminal velocity.
lessons.content_html:
Speed and Velocity

Speed tells you how fast an object is moving. It is a scalar quantity — it has magnitude but no direction. The equation linking distance, speed and time is:

$$s = v \times t$$

Where \(s\) is distance (m), \(v\) is speed (m/s), and \(t\) is time (s). You can rearrange this to find speed (\(v = \frac{s}{t}\)) or time (\(t = \frac{s}{v}\)). Typical speeds to know: walking (~1.5 m/s), running (~3 m/s), cycling (~6 m/s), a car in town (~13 m/s), and the speed of sound in air (~340 m/s).

Velocity is speed in a stated direction. It is a vector quantity. An object travelling in a circle at constant speed has a changing velocity because its direction constantly changes — meaning it is always accelerating, even though its speed stays the same.

Similarly, distance (scalar) measures total ground covered, while displacement (vector) measures how far and in what direction from the start. A runner completing a 400 m lap of a track covers a distance of 400 m but has a displacement of zero — they end up back where they started.

Key Fact

Speed and distance are scalars (magnitude only). Velocity and displacement are vectors (magnitude + direction). An object moving in a circle at constant speed has a changing velocity because direction constantly changes.

Acceleration

Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes. An object accelerates when it speeds up, slows down, or changes direction. The equation is:

$$a = \frac{v - u}{t}$$

Where \(a\) is acceleration (m/s2), \(v\) is final velocity (m/s), \(u\) is initial velocity (m/s), and \(t\) is time (s). A negative value means the object is decelerating. For example, a car braking from 20 m/s to rest in 5 s has an acceleration of \(a = \frac{0 - 20}{5} = -4 \text{ m/s}^2\).

Question: A cyclist accelerates from 2 m/s to 14 m/s in 6 seconds. Calculate her acceleration.

Step 1: Identify values: \(u = 2 \text{ m/s}\), \(v = 14 \text{ m/s}\), \(t = 6 \text{ s}\).

Step 2: Apply the equation: \(a = \frac{v - u}{t} = \frac{14 - 2}{6} = \frac{12}{6} = 2 \text{ m/s}^2\)

Note: Always include units in your final answer. Forgetting units is one of the most common reasons for losing marks on calculation questions.

Distance-Time Graphs

On a distance-time graph, time is always plotted on the x-axis and distance on the y-axis. The gradient (slope) of the line gives the speed. You can read the shape of the line as follows:

• A horizontal line means the object is stationary (speed = 0).
• A straight diagonal line means constant speed — steeper gradient means greater speed.
• A curve getting steeper means the object is accelerating.
• A curve getting shallower means the object is decelerating.

To find the speed at a specific instant on a curved distance-time graph, draw a tangent to the curve at that point and calculate its gradient.

Key Fact

On a distance-time graph: gradient = speed. On a velocity-time graph: gradient = acceleration. Time is always on the x-axis for motion graphs. Plotting them the wrong way round is a common exam error.

Velocity-Time Graphs

On a velocity-time graph, two key pieces of information can be extracted:

• The gradient equals the acceleration. A steeper slope means greater acceleration. A horizontal line means constant velocity (zero acceleration). A downward slope means deceleration.
• A line below the x-axis means the object is moving in the opposite direction.

The area under the line on a velocity-time graph equals the distance travelled. For a triangle, the area is \(\frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}\). For a rectangle, it is base × height. For irregular shapes, split into triangles and rectangles and add them together.

To measure the speed of a trolley rolling down a ramp, mark a measured distance on the ramp. Use a stopwatch to time how long the trolley takes to travel between two marked points, then calculate speed using \(v = \frac{s}{t}\). For greater precision, use light gates connected to a data logger — these measure very short time intervals as the trolley interrupts the beam, allowing you to calculate instantaneous speed. Using two light gates at different positions lets you compare speeds and calculate acceleration.

Terminal Velocity

When an object falls through a fluid (such as air or water), two forces act on it: its weight (downwards) and drag (upwards, opposing motion). Initially, weight is much greater than drag, so the object accelerates downwards. As speed increases, drag increases. Eventually, drag equals weight. At this point the resultant force is zero and the object reaches terminal velocity.

A skydiver provides a clear example. After jumping, they accelerate rapidly. As speed builds, air resistance increases until it equals their weight — this is their first terminal velocity (around 55 m/s for a spread-eagled position). When the parachute opens, surface area dramatically increases, causing air resistance to suddenly far exceed weight. The skydiver decelerates until a new, much lower terminal velocity is reached (around 5–7 m/s), safe for landing.

On a velocity-time graph, terminal velocity appears as a curve that starts steep (rapid acceleration) and gradually flattens out to a horizontal line (constant velocity). The curve of a parachute opening would show a sharp decrease in velocity before levelling off again at the lower terminal speed.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For motion graph questions, always label your axes with both the quantity and the unit (e.g. “time / s”, “velocity / m/s”) — missing units on axes costs marks. Time must always go on the x-axis for motion graphs. When asked to “describe the motion”, refer to the gradient explicitly: “the gradient is decreasing, so the object is decelerating.” For extended responses on terminal velocity, make sure you state that the resultant force is zero, not just that “forces are equal” — the command word “explain” requires the link between zero resultant force and zero acceleration.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Speed and distance are scalars; velocity and displacement are vectors. Acceleration = rate of change of velocity, calculated using \(a = \frac{v-u}{t}\). Always include units in your answer.
  • On a distance-time graph, gradient = speed (time on x-axis always). On a velocity-time graph, gradient = acceleration; area under line = distance. Horizontal line = constant velocity (not necessarily stationary).
  • Terminal velocity is reached when drag equals weight (resultant force = zero, acceleration = zero). A parachute increases drag, producing a lower second terminal velocity safe for landing.

lessons.title: Newton's Laws and Resultant Forces
lessons.description: Newton's three laws, F = ma calculations, inertial mass, weight versus mass, and stopping distances.
lessons.content_html:
Newton’s First Law

Newton’s First Law states that an object remains at rest or continues to move at constant velocity unless acted upon by a resultant force. This means:

• If the resultant force is zero, a stationary object stays still and a moving object keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction.
• If there is a resultant force, the object accelerates — which means it speeds up, slows down, or changes direction.

A spacecraft drifting in deep space continues at the same velocity indefinitely because there is no friction or air resistance to produce a resultant force. A book on a table remains stationary because the normal contact force from the table (upward) exactly balances its weight (downward).

Key Fact

Objects do not need a force to keep moving at constant velocity. A resultant force is only needed to change the speed or direction of an object. Zero resultant force → no change in motion.

Newton’s Second Law: F = ma

Newton’s Second Law states that the resultant force on an object is equal to its mass multiplied by its acceleration:

$$F = m \times a$$

Where \(F\) is resultant force (N), \(m\) is mass (kg), and \(a\) is acceleration (m/s2). The equation shows that a larger force produces a larger acceleration for the same mass, and a larger mass requires a larger force for the same acceleration. Remember: \(F\) is always the resultant force, not just any single force acting on the object.

Question: A car engine provides 4 200 N of driving force. Friction and air resistance total 1 400 N. The car has a mass of 700 kg. Calculate its acceleration.

Step 1: Find the resultant force: \(F = 4200 - 1400 = 2800 \text{ N}\)

Step 2: Apply Newton’s Second Law: \(a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{2800}{700} = 4 \text{ m/s}^2\)

You can investigate Newton’s Second Law using a trolley on a smooth track with a string passing over a pulley to a hanging mass. The hanging mass provides the driving force. Use light gates to measure acceleration. Keep the total mass of the system constant and vary the force by moving masses from the trolley to the hanger. Plot force against acceleration — a straight line through the origin confirms \(F \propto a\) at constant mass.

Weight, Mass and Gravitational Field Strength

Mass is the amount of matter in an object. It is measured in kg and does not change with location. Weight is the force of gravity acting on that mass, measured in newtons. The equation is:

$$W = m \times g$$

Where \(W\) is weight (N), \(m\) is mass (kg) and \(g\) is gravitational field strength (N/kg). At the Earth’s surface, \(g = 10 \text{ N/kg}\). A 70 kg person weighs 700 N on Earth but would weigh only about 112 N on the Moon, where \(g \approx 1.6 \text{ N/kg}\). Their mass stays at 70 kg in both locations. The numerical value of \(g\) at the Earth’s surface also equals the acceleration due to gravity in free fall (\(10 \text{ m/s}^2\)).

Inertial Mass

Inertial mass is defined as the ratio of the resultant force applied to an object to the acceleration it produces:

$$m = \frac{F}{a}$$

This is Newton’s Second Law rearranged. An object with greater inertial mass is harder to accelerate for the same applied force. Inertial mass and gravitational mass (the mass that determines how strongly gravity pulls an object) have the same value — this equivalence is a fundamental feature of physics and was central to Einstein’s thinking, though it is not required beyond GCSE level.

Newton’s Third Law

Newton’s Third Law states: for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. These action-reaction pairs always act on different objects and are always the same type of force. For example:

• When you push a wall, the wall pushes back on you with an equal force in the opposite direction (both are normal contact forces).
• When the Earth pulls you downwards by gravity (your weight), you pull the Earth upwards with an equal gravitational force.
• A swimmer pushes water backwards — the water pushes the swimmer forwards.

A common mistake is to treat weight and the normal contact force as a Third Law pair. They are not — both act on the same object. A true Third Law pair involves forces on different objects.

Key Fact

Newton’s Third Law pairs: equal in size, opposite in direction, same type of force, acting on different objects. If both forces act on the same object, they are NOT a Third Law pair.

Stopping Distance

The total stopping distance of a vehicle is the sum of the thinking distance and the braking distance. Thinking distance is the distance covered from when the driver sees a hazard to when the brakes are applied. Braking distance is the distance covered while the brakes are applied and the vehicle slows to a stop.

• Factors increasing thinking distance: higher speed, tiredness, alcohol, drugs, distractions such as a mobile phone.
• Factors increasing braking distance: higher speed (braking distance is proportional to speed squared, so doubling speed quadruples braking distance), wet or icy roads, worn tyres, poorly maintained brakes, larger mass of vehicle.
• Speed affects both: at higher speed the vehicle covers more ground during the reaction time and also needs more braking distance to decelerate from a higher initial velocity.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions on stopping distance, always distinguish clearly between thinking distance and braking distance — examiners penalise conflating the two. For F = ma calculations, always work out the resultant force first before substituting; a common error is using the engine force alone when resistive forces are given. For Newton’s Third Law questions, check that your pair of forces acts on two different objects and is the same type of force — if both forces act on the same object, they are simply a balanced pair, not a Third Law pair.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Newton’s First Law: objects keep the same velocity unless a resultant force acts. Newton’s Second Law: \(F = ma\) where F is the resultant force. Newton’s Third Law: action-reaction forces are equal, opposite, same type, and act on different objects.
  • Weight = mass × gravitational field strength (\(W = mg\)). Mass is constant regardless of location; weight changes with gravitational field strength. On Earth, \(g = 10 \text{ N/kg}\).
  • Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. Speed increases both. Reaction time affects thinking distance; road and vehicle conditions affect braking distance.

lessons.title: Forces in Action: Springs, Hooke's Law and Moments
lessons.description: Hooke's law for springs, elastic and plastic deformation, elastic potential energy, moments, levers and gears.
lessons.content_html:
Elastic and Plastic Deformation

To stretch, bend or compress an object, more than one force must be applied. A single force would simply cause the object to accelerate (Newton’s Second Law). Two opposing forces are required for deformation — for example, a weight pulling a spring downwards while the support holds it up.

When forces are applied to a spring, it can undergo two types of deformation:

• Elastic deformation — the object returns to its original shape when the force is removed. The spring ‘bounces back.’
• Plastic deformation — the object is permanently deformed. The spring has been stretched beyond its elastic limit and does not recover.

Hooke’s Law

Hooke’s Law states that the extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied, as long as the elastic limit is not exceeded. The equation is:

$$F = k \times e$$

Where \(F\) is force (N), \(k\) is the spring constant (N/m), and \(e\) is extension (m). Extension is the change in length: \(e = \text{stretched length} - \text{natural length}\). A larger spring constant means a stiffer spring. On a force-extension graph, the straight-line region confirms Hooke’s Law; the gradient of this line equals the spring constant \(k\). Beyond the elastic limit, the graph curves — deformation becomes plastic.

Key Fact

Hooke’s Law: \(F = ke\). The gradient of the straight-line section of a force-extension graph equals the spring constant \(k\). Beyond the elastic limit, deformation is plastic and permanent.

Clamp a spring vertically from a stand. Measure and record the natural length using a ruler. Add known masses one at a time, recording the total length each time. Calculate extension for each mass (\(e = \text{new length} - \text{natural length}\)). Plot force (y-axis) against extension (x-axis). The straight-line section confirms Hooke’s Law; the point where the line begins to curve marks the elastic limit. To improve accuracy, take repeated readings at each force and calculate the mean; read the ruler at eye level to avoid parallax; ensure the spring hangs freely without touching the stand.

When a spring is stretched elastically, energy is stored as elastic potential energy (EPE):

$$E_e = \frac{1}{2} \times k \times e^2$$

Where \(E_e\) is elastic potential energy (J), \(k\) is the spring constant (N/m), and \(e\) is extension (m). This equation only applies within the elastic limit (the linear region). On a force-extension graph, the EPE equals the triangular area under the straight-line section: \(\frac{1}{2} \times F \times e\). When the spring is released, this stored energy is transferred to kinetic energy or gravitational potential energy.

Moments

A moment is the turning effect of a force about a pivot. It is calculated using:

$$M = F \times d$$

Where \(M\) is the moment (N m), \(F\) is the force (N), and \(d\) is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force (m). The distance must be perpendicular to the force — using a slanted distance gives the wrong answer. Moments are measured in newton-metres (N m).

For an object to be in rotational equilibrium, the total clockwise moment about any pivot must equal the total anticlockwise moment about the same pivot. This is the principle of moments:

$$\text{total clockwise moment} = \text{total anticlockwise moment}$$

Question: A see-saw has a pivot at its centre. A child of weight 300 N sits 1.5 m from the pivot on the left. How far from the pivot must a 450 N adult sit on the right to balance the see-saw?

Step 1: Anticlockwise moment (child) = \(300 \times 1.5 = 450 \text{ N m}\).

Step 2: For equilibrium: clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment.
\(450 \times d = 450\)
\(d = 450 \div 450 = 1.0 \text{ m}\).

The adult must sit 1.0 m from the pivot. Notice that the heavier person sits closer to the pivot to produce the same moment.

Key Fact

Moment (N m) = Force (N) × perpendicular distance from pivot (m). For equilibrium: total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment (principle of moments). Distance must be perpendicular to the force.

Levers and Gears

A lever uses the principle of moments to act as a force multiplier. By applying a small effort at a large distance from the pivot, you can overcome a larger load closer to the pivot. For example, a crowbar enables a small downward push to lift a large rock. Scissors, tweezers, a bottle opener and a wheelbarrow are all examples of levers in different configurations.

The key idea: the lever multiplies force because moment = force × distance. If the effort arm is longer than the load arm, the effort force needed is smaller than the load force, even though both produce equal moments.

Gears are toothed wheels that mesh together and transmit turning forces. When two gears of different sizes mesh:

• The smaller gear turns faster but with less force (smaller moment).
• The larger gear turns more slowly but with greater force (larger moment).
• The number of teeth on each gear determines the gear ratio — larger gear ÷ smaller gear. A higher gear ratio means a greater increase in force but a reduction in speed.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For Hooke’s Law questions, remember: extension is the change in length, not the total stretched length. In moments calculations, the distance must always be perpendicular to the force — a diagram often helps you identify this. For force-extension graph questions, the elastic limit is where the graph first curves away from the straight line; make sure you identify this point clearly. When asked to describe plastic deformation, state that the object “does not return to its original shape when the force is removed” — vague answers like “stretches too far” will not gain marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hooke’s Law: \(F = ke\). Extension is proportional to force up to the elastic limit. Beyond this, deformation is plastic (permanent). The gradient of the force-extension graph’s straight section = spring constant k.
  • Moment = force × perpendicular distance from pivot (unit: N m). For rotational equilibrium, total clockwise moments = total anticlockwise moments (principle of moments).
  • Levers act as force multipliers using the principle of moments. Gears transmit turning forces; a larger gear turns slower but produces a greater turning effect.

lessons.title: Static Electricity and Simple Circuits
lessons.description: Charge transfer, electric fields, current, potential difference, resistance, Ohm's law, and I-V characteristics.
lessons.content_html:
Static Electricity

Charge is a fundamental property of all matter. In most objects, the number of positive charges equals the number of negative charges, so the object is electrically neutral. When two insulating materials are rubbed together, friction causes electrons to transfer from one surface to the other, creating static electricity.

The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged. The material that loses electrons becomes positively charged. It is always the electrons that move — protons are locked inside the nucleus and cannot transfer between objects. For example, when a polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth, electrons move from the cloth to the rod: the rod becomes negative and the cloth becomes positive.

Static charge builds up only on insulators because electrons cannot flow away through the material. On a conductor, any excess charge spreads out immediately. If enough charge accumulates, it can discharge as a spark — this is what causes lightning.

Key Fact

Static electricity is caused by the transfer of electrons between insulating materials. An object becomes positive by losing electrons — not by gaining positive charges. Protons never move between objects.

Electric Fields

A charged object creates an electric field in the space around it. Electric field lines show the direction a positive charge would move if placed in the field — they point away from positive charges and towards negative charges. Where field lines are closer together, the field is stronger.

Two charged objects exert forces on each other through their electric fields — like charges repel and unlike charges attract. This force acts even without the objects touching, which is why a charged balloon can attract small pieces of paper without contact.

Current, Charge and Potential Difference

Current is the rate of flow of charge through a conductor. For current to flow, there must be a source of potential difference and a complete (closed) circuit. The equation linking charge, current and time is:

$$Q = I \times t$$

Where \(Q\) is charge (coulombs, C), \(I\) is current (amperes, A), and \(t\) is time (seconds, s). In a series circuit, current is the same at every point because charge is not used up. Current is measured with an ammeter in series; potential difference is measured with a voltmeter in parallel across the component.

Resistance and Ohm’s Law

Resistance opposes the flow of current. The greater the resistance, the smaller the current for a given potential difference. The relationship is:

$$V = I \times R$$

Where \(V\) is potential difference (V), \(I\) is current (A), and \(R\) is resistance (Ω). Ohm’s Law states that current is directly proportional to potential difference, provided temperature remains constant. This applies only to ohmic conductors — components whose resistance stays constant.

Key Fact

\(V = IR\) links potential difference, current and resistance. Ohm’s Law: current is proportional to PD only if temperature is constant (ohmic conductor). Current measured by ammeter in series; PD by voltmeter in parallel.

Set up a circuit with a variable resistor, ammeter in series, and voltmeter in parallel across the component under test. Adjust the variable resistor to change the current; record both current and potential difference at each setting. Plot an I-V graph (current on y-axis, potential difference on x-axis). For a resistor at constant temperature, the graph is a straight line through the origin — confirming Ohm’s Law. Repeat with a filament lamp and a diode to compare their I-V characteristics.

I-V Characteristics

An I-V characteristic graph shows how current varies with potential difference for a component. You need to know the shape for three key components (PAG P7):

• Fixed resistor (ohmic conductor): a straight line through the origin. Gradient is constant, so resistance is constant. Obeys Ohm’s Law.
• Filament lamp: an S-shaped curve that starts steep (low resistance when cool) and flattens as PD increases (higher resistance as the filament heats up). As current increases, the filament temperature rises, so resistance increases. The curve is symmetrical in forward and reverse directions.
• Diode: current only flows in one direction (the forward direction). In the reverse direction, resistance is very high and virtually no current flows. There is a threshold voltage (roughly 0.6 V for a silicon diode) below which even forward current is negligible.

Some components have resistance that changes with environmental conditions:

• A light-dependent resistor (LDR) has high resistance in the dark and low resistance in bright light. Used in automatic streetlights and burglar alarms.
• An NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient) has high resistance when cold and low resistance when hot. Used in thermostats, fire alarms, and engine management systems.
Both are used in potential divider circuits where their changing resistance produces a varying output voltage that depends on light level or temperature.

Key Fact

I-V graph shapes: resistor = straight line (constant resistance, obeys Ohm’s Law); filament lamp = curve (resistance increases with temperature); diode = conducts in one direction only.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about static electricity, always state that electrons transfer — never protons or positive charges. For I-V graph questions, explain the shape by linking it to resistance and temperature (for the lamp) or the one-way nature of current flow (for the diode). For calculation questions using \(V = IR\), always identify which value you are solving for and rearrange the equation before substituting numbers. A common error is using the wrong value for current when the ammeter is in parallel — remember, the ammeter must always be in series.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Static electricity is caused by electron transfer between insulators. Only electrons move — positive charges never transfer. Like charges repel; unlike charges attract. Charge creates an electric field in the surrounding space.
  • Current (A) = charge (C) ÷ time (s). Resistance opposes current. Ohm’s Law: \(V = IR\) applies when temperature is constant. Ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel.
  • I-V graph shapes: fixed resistor = straight line; filament lamp = S-curve (resistance increases with temperature); diode = one-way conduction only. LDR and thermistor resistance changes with light and temperature.

lessons.title: Series, Parallel and Domestic Electricity
lessons.description: Series and parallel circuit rules, mains AC vs battery DC, plug wiring, electrical power, and the National Grid.
lessons.content_html:
Series and Parallel Circuits

In a series circuit, all components are in a single continuous loop. This means:

• Current is the same at every point in the circuit — charge is not used up.
• Potential difference is shared between components — the sum of individual voltages equals the supply voltage.
• Total resistance = sum of individual resistances: \(R_{\text{total}} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3\)
• If one component fails, the circuit breaks and all components stop working.

In a parallel circuit, components are on separate branches. This means:

• Potential difference is the same across each branch (and equals the supply voltage).
• Current splits between branches — more current flows through the branch with lower resistance.
• Total resistance is lower than the smallest individual resistance because there are more paths for current.
• If one component fails, the others continue to work. This is why household appliances use parallel wiring.

Key Fact

Series: current the same everywhere; PD shared. Parallel: PD the same across each branch; current shared. Adding resistors in parallel decreases total resistance (more paths available).

Series: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 4 Ω in series: \(R_{\text{total}} = 6 + 4 = 10 \text{ } \Omega\). If the supply is 20 V, the current everywhere is \(I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{20}{10} = 2 \text{ A}\). The 6 Ω resistor has \(V = 2 \times 6 = 12 \text{ V}\) across it; the 4 Ω resistor has \(V = 2 \times 4 = 8 \text{ V}\). Sum: \(12 + 8 = 20 \text{ V}\) ✓

Parallel: Two 6 Ω resistors in parallel. Each has 12 V across it. Current in each branch: \(I = \frac{12}{6} = 2 \text{ A}\). Total current from supply: \(2 + 2 = 4 \text{ A}\). Effective total resistance: \(R = \frac{12}{4} = 3 \text{ } \Omega\) — lower than either individual resistor.

AC and DC

Direct current (DC) flows in one direction only — this is what batteries and solar cells produce. Alternating current (AC) constantly reverses direction. The UK mains supply is AC at a frequency of 50 Hz (50 complete cycles per second) and a voltage of about 230 V. On an oscilloscope trace, AC appears as a sine wave oscillating above and below zero; DC appears as a flat horizontal line.

Key Fact

UK domestic mains: AC at 230 V and 50 Hz. Batteries: DC. AC can have its voltage changed by a transformer; DC cannot. On an oscilloscope trace: AC = wave, DC = flat line.

Mains Wiring and Safety

A UK three-pin plug contains three wires, each with a specific colour and function:

• Live (brown) — carries the AC supply at about 230 V. Always dangerous, even when the appliance is switched off, because it remains connected to the mains supply.
• Neutral (blue) — completes the circuit at approximately 0 V. Current flows in through the live and out through the neutral.
• Earth (green and yellow striped) — a safety wire connected to the metal casing of an appliance. Provides a low-resistance path to earth if a fault causes the casing to become live.

A fuse is always in the live wire. If the current exceeds the fuse rating, the fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit, preventing overheating or fire. The earth wire and fuse work together: if the live wire accidentally touches the metal casing, a surge of current flows through the earth wire, blowing the fuse and cutting the supply. A residual current device (RCD) provides faster protection by detecting any imbalance between live and neutral currents and cutting the circuit within milliseconds.

Appliances with plastic casings (such as hairdryers and power drills) use double insulation. The plastic casing cannot become live because it is an insulator, so there is no risk of the user receiving an electric shock even if the wiring inside develops a fault. These appliances are marked with a double-square symbol and do not require an earth wire. This makes them safe in damp environments where a metal-cased appliance with a faulty earth could be particularly dangerous.

Electrical Power and Energy

Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer. The key equations are:

$$P = V \times I \qquad P = I^2 \times R$$

Where \(P\) is power (W), \(V\) is potential difference (V), \(I\) is current (A), and \(R\) is resistance (Ω). The second equation is useful when voltage is not known. The total energy transferred is:

$$E = P \times t$$

Where \(E\) is energy (J) and \(t\) is time (s). For domestic billing, energy is measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh): one kWh = a 1 kW appliance running for 1 hour. Cost = energy (kWh) × price per kWh.

Key Fact

Power equations: \(P = VI\), \(P = I^2R\). Energy transferred: \(E = Pt\). Domestic energy unit: kilowatt-hour (kWh). Cost (pence) = energy (kWh) × price per unit.

The National Grid

The National Grid transmits electricity from power stations to consumers across the UK. Electricity is transmitted at very high voltages (up to several hundred thousand volts) and correspondingly low currents to minimise energy losses in the cables. Since the power wasted as heat in cables is \(P_{\text{loss}} = I^2 R\), a smaller current dramatically reduces losses — squaring the current means even a small reduction in current makes a large difference.

Step-up transformers at power stations increase voltage (and reduce current) for long-distance transmission. Step-down transformers at local substations reduce the voltage to 230 V for safe household use. Transformers only work with AC because they rely on a changing magnetic field in the core to induce a voltage in the secondary coil; a DC supply would produce a constant field and no induced voltage.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For circuit questions, always identify whether the circuit is series or parallel before applying any rules. A common error is assuming that adding more components always increases resistance — this is only true in series; in parallel, adding more branches decreases total resistance. For plug wiring questions, learn the colour codes: live = brown, neutral = blue, earth = green/yellow. For National Grid questions, always explain that high voltage means low current, and link this to \(P = I^2R\) to show why lower current reduces heat losses.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Series circuits: current the same throughout; PD shared; total resistance = sum of individual resistances. Parallel circuits: PD the same across each branch; current shared; total resistance is less than any individual branch.
  • UK mains supply: AC at 230 V, 50 Hz. Plug: live (brown) at 230 V, neutral (blue) at 0 V, earth (green/yellow) for safety. Fuse always in the live wire. Power: \(P = VI\) or \(P = I^2R\).
  • The National Grid transmits at high voltage / low current to minimise heat losses (\(P = I^2R\)). Step-up transformers increase voltage for transmission; step-down transformers reduce it for domestic use. Transformers only work with AC.

lessons.content_html:
Permanent and Induced Magnets

A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field continuously. It has a north pole and a south pole. The fundamental rule of magnetism is: like poles repel; unlike poles attract. Common permanent magnet materials include iron, steel, nickel and cobalt — these are called magnetic materials.

An induced magnet only becomes magnetic while inside another magnetic field. When the external field is removed, it loses its magnetism. An induced magnet is always attracted to the permanent magnet that magnetises it — never repelled — because the induced poles always arrange themselves so that unlike poles face each other. This is how a permanent magnet can pick up an iron nail.

Key Fact

Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. A permanent magnet always has its own field. An induced magnet is temporary — it is always attracted to the magnet that magnetises it because unlike poles always face each other.

Magnetic Fields

A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where a magnetic force is exerted. Field lines represent the field:

• Field lines run from north to south outside the magnet.
• Closer field lines indicate a stronger field.
• The field is strongest at the poles.
• Field lines never cross each other.

You can map a magnetic field using a plotting compass: place it near the magnet, mark where the needle points, move the compass to the new position and repeat. Alternatively, sprinkle iron filings around a magnet — they align along field lines, revealing the pattern. The Earth itself produces a magnetic field, generated by convection currents in its liquid iron outer core, which is why a compass needle points towards geographic north.

When current flows through a straight wire, a weak circular magnetic field forms around it. A solenoid is a wire wound into a coil. The individual circular fields from each loop combine to produce a strong, uniform field inside the coil, with a distinct north and south pole at each end — just like a bar magnet.

Adding a soft iron core inside the solenoid creates an electromagnet. The iron core becomes a strong induced magnet and greatly amplifies the field. The strength of an electromagnet increases with: a larger current, more turns in the coil, and a soft iron core. Crucially, an electromagnet can be switched on and off by controlling the current. Applications include: scrapyard lifting cranes, electric bells, relays, loudspeakers, and MRI scanners.

The Motor Effect

When a current-carrying conductor is placed in an external magnetic field, it experiences a force. This is the motor effect. The force is greatest when the current is perpendicular to the field, and zero when they are parallel.

The equation for the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is:

$$F = B \times I \times l$$

Where \(F\) is force (N), \(B\) is magnetic flux density (T, tesla), \(I\) is current (A), and \(l\) is the length of the conductor within the field (m). Increasing the field strength, current, or length of wire all produce a greater force.

Fleming’s Left-Hand Rule

Fleming’s left-hand rule determines the direction of the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field. Hold the left hand with thumb, first finger and second finger all at right angles to each other:

• Thumb = Force (direction of motion/thrust).
• First finger = Field direction (north to south).
• Second finger = Current direction (conventional current, positive to negative).

A useful mnemonic: thuMb = Motion, First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current. Reversing any one of the three reverses the corresponding direction of the force.

Key Fact

Motor effect: \(F = BIl\). Fleming’s left-hand rule: Thumb = Force, First finger = Field (N to S), Second finger = Current (+ to −). The motor effect is the operating principle of electric motors.

In a simple DC motor, a current-carrying coil sits in the field between two permanent magnets. The two sides of the coil experience forces in opposite directions (because the current flows in opposite directions on each side). This creates a turning effect — the coil rotates. A split-ring commutator reverses the current through the coil every half turn, ensuring the forces always act in the same rotational direction and the coil spins continuously.

Electromagnetic Induction

The motor effect works in reverse: moving a conductor through a magnetic field (or changing the magnetic field through a conductor) generates an induced potential difference, and if the circuit is complete, a current flows. This is electromagnetic induction. The size of the induced potential difference depends on: the speed of movement, the strength of the magnetic field, and the number of turns in the coil. Reversing the direction of movement reverses the direction of the induced current.

This principle underlies generators (which convert kinetic energy to electrical energy) and transformers (which transfer electrical energy between circuits via a changing magnetic field). In a generator, a coil rotates within a magnetic field; the changing flux through the coil induces an alternating potential difference. In a transformer, the changing current in the primary coil creates a changing magnetic field in the iron core, which induces a voltage in the secondary coil.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For motor effect questions, practise Fleming’s left-hand rule until it becomes automatic — point your fingers in the directions given and use the remaining finger to identify the unknown quantity. A common error is using the right-hand rule (which applies to generators, not motors). For electromagnetic induction extended responses, make sure you state that a changing magnetic field is required — a static field produces no induced voltage. Always link the direction of induced current to Lenz’s Law qualitatively: the induced current opposes the change that caused it.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. Permanent magnets always have their own field. Induced magnets are temporary and always attracted to the magnet that creates them. Solenoids with soft iron cores create electromagnets that can be switched on and off.
  • The motor effect: a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force. \(F = BIl\). Direction given by Fleming’s left-hand rule (thumb = force, first finger = field, second finger = current).
  • Electromagnetic induction: moving a conductor through a field (or changing the field) induces a potential difference. This principle underlies generators and transformers. A changing magnetic field — not a static one — is required.

glossary_terms.definition: A magnet that produces its own magnetic field at all times, without needing an external current or field.
Materials that are attracted to magnets and can be magnetised, including iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.
A magnetic material that becomes a temporary magnet when placed in a magnetic field, losing its magnetism when the external field is removed.
The region around a magnet where a magnetic material or a moving charge experiences a force.
A coil of wire that produces a strong magnetic field when current flows through it, similar in shape to a bar magnet's field.
A solenoid with a soft iron core that greatly strengthens the magnetic field. The magnetism can be switched on and off by controlling the current.
The force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field. The force is perpendicular to both the current direction and the field direction.
A measure of the strength of a magnetic field, measured in tesla (T). A stronger field has a higher flux density.

A rule for finding the direction of force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field: thumb = force (motion), first finger = field direction (N to S), second finger = conventional current direction.
The process by which a changing magnetic field through a conductor generates a potential difference (and a current if the circuit is complete). This is the reverse of the motor effect.
